The mines were deep below Arsenal. Drums beat loud and low, bored from great trees larger than a man. With the skins stretched taut against the bore, their beats sounded loud through the mines and some say they sounded through rock and stone itself. It was cool and damp in the deep, and against the tolling of the picks against rough-hewn rock walls the sounds of the mines blended into a low drone that lulled you into comfort, saying, *come work, swing a pick against the stone, come to the deep*. Many fell to this urge and began to work in the mines. Some returned, but for the rest of their lives they could never quite shake the urge to go back to the deep, working alongside others in the light of a flickering oil lamp digging tunnels to nowhere.

It was time to expand the mine. The central shaft, a massive borehole more than three hundred feet wide studded with countless catwalks and scaffolds and stairs going up and down and every which way, had become perforated with countless tunnels leading off in every possible direction. There was no room to build new tunnels - other than down. Picks made holes in the ground, and into the holes were packed charges of gunpowder. Fuses were lit, and they ran. The rock sheared, slabs were hauled off, and the process repeated again and again and again. The fuses were lit again, and the gunpowder exploded. The floor caved in and twenty miners could do nothing but run on air and plunge to their death. When the dust cloud cleared, a torch was thrown down. It splashed into a massive underground lake, and as the echoes subsided they could hear the joyous calls for help from the miners.

A long rope was thrown down, and ten miners were pulled up. No more survived from the fall into the lake. They told of how far the fall was, more than five hundred feet down to the deep pool of water that saved their lives. The other miners resumed their duties, building scaffolds and tunneling into the face of the shaft, but the call to the deep was stronger than ever before. Eventually an exploration party was sent down in a boat suspended from one of the mine cranes. Three days they were in the cavern, three days no word was heard. Three days until a signal was sent up and they were hauled back up to the surface. They told of seemingly endless natural tunnels that led to a massive underground network of caves and shafts. Once they came up aboveground from a cave twenty miles from Arsenal when they swore they only walked ten. Soon a platform was lowered to the lake and anchored by pylons to its bed, and scaffolding from the mines to the cavern went up. Bridges were built to the shore, and soon all the people of Arsenal were exploring this brave new land. Buildings went up on the shore and in the shallows of the lake, inns and shops and smithies serving the new adventurers-to-be that delved deep into the new place they called the Underlands.

On the shores of the lake they now called Lithia, in the town they called Barrowhelm, rifts began to form in the populace. Guilds formed, all dedicated in one way or another to use of the Underlands, all perpetually treading on one anothers' toes. Two adventuring guilds, the Hvennholl and the Svilderholl, warred against each other to see who could traverse the Underlands better, who could find lost treasures and slay legendary beings. Of course, neither guild could prove either of those existed. Some say that there is power beyond imagine in the Underlands, riches beyond measure and lost beings guarding them. Of course, some say nothing waits but death...
